overview.text: The Battle of France was Germany’s rapid defeat of France and its allies in May and June 1940. German forces attacked the Low Countries on 10 May, drawing British and French armies into Belgium, while the main armored thrust crossed the Ardennes farther south. The breakthrough reached the coast and trapped Allied troops in the north; many escaped by sea from Dunkirk. German troops entered Paris on 14 June, and France signed an armistice on 22 June. Germany occupied much of France, while a French government based at Vichy cooperated with it. The campaign dramatically changed World War II by removing Britain’s principal continental ally.

key_facts.text: Germany opened its western offensive on 10 May 1940.
The main German attack passed through the Ardennes.
More than 300,000 French and British troops escaped via Dunkirk.
Paris fell on 14 June; France signed an armistice on 22 June.
The Vichy government was led by Marshal Philippe Pétain.

overview.text: The 2019–2020 Hong Kong protests began after the city’s government proposed an extradition bill that could have sent suspects to mainland China. Huge marches in 2019 pressed for the bill’s withdrawal, but the movement broadened into demands for an independent inquiry into police conduct, release of arrested protesters, and democratic elections. The government withdrew the bill, yet protests and arguments over civil liberties continued. Police and demonstrators clashed during parts of the movement, alongside many peaceful marches. In June 2020, China imposed a national security law on Hong Kong, changing the political setting in which activists operated. The movement became a major contest over Hong Kong’s autonomy and freedoms.

key_facts.text: The proposed 2019 bill would have allowed extradition to mainland China.
The bill’s withdrawal was one of the movement’s five demands.
Protesters sought an independent inquiry into police use of force.
They also called for genuine universal suffrage.
China imposed a Hong Kong national security law on 30 June 2020.

overview.text: Jesuit reductions were mission settlements established among Indigenous peoples in colonial South America, especially among the Guaraní. Jesuit priests sought to spread Catholic Christianity while Guaraní residents lived, worked, and maintained parts of their language and culture within the settlements. The reductions had churches, houses, workshops, ranches, and cultivated land; cattle raising and yerba mate contributed to their economies. Local councils involved Guaraní leaders, although priests retained considerable authority over daily life. The settlements formed part of the Spanish colonial world rather than an independent state. Spain expelled the Jesuits from its territories in 1767, and the mission system changed after their departure. Ruins in Argentina and Brazil are protected as World Heritage sites.

key_facts.text: The missions were part of Jesuit evangelization among Guaraní communities.
Some reductions raised cattle and traded yerba mate.
Settlements included churches, housing, workshops, and farmland.
Guaraní leaders participated in local councils, while priests retained authority.
Spain ordered the Jesuits expelled from its domains in 1767.

overview.text: Mozambique is a country in southern Africa that became independent from Portugal in 1975 after negotiations involving FRELIMO. Independence did not bring lasting peace. The FRELIMO-led government fought the armed RENAMO movement in a long civil war that brought severe hardship to the country. Leaders of the government and RENAMO signed a General Peace Agreement in Rome on 4 October 1992. A United Nations mission then helped monitor the ceasefire, demobilization, and elections. The country’s history therefore includes both a struggle against colonial rule and a difficult transition from civil war to multiparty politics.

FRELIMO negotiated the transition from Portuguese rule.
The civil war pitted the FRELIMO-led government against RENAMO.

overview.text: The Battle of Leuctra in 371 BCE was a decisive Theban victory over a Spartan-led army in ancient Greece. Theban commander Epaminondas concentrated his hoplites in an unusually deep formation on the left, opposite the Spartan king Cleombrotus. Contemporary writer Xenophon describes the Theban line as at least fifty shields deep and the Spartan line as no more than twelve. Theban cavalry helped disrupt the Spartan advance, and Cleombrotus died during the fighting. The defeat shattered Sparta’s reputation for battlefield dominance and opened a period of greater Theban power. Historians debate some details of the battle, but its importance as a turning point is clear.

Epaminondas commanded the victorious Theban forces.
Theban hoplites massed at least fifty shields deep, according to Xenophon.
Spartan king Cleombrotus died during the battle.

overview.text: The Medici were a Florentine family of merchants and bankers whose wealth gave them great political influence during the Renaissance. In the fifteenth century they dominated Florence without holding a formal hereditary title; later members ruled as dukes and grand dukes. Their support for artists and scholars helped make Florence a center of Renaissance art and humanist learning. Lorenzo de’ Medici was among the family’s best-known patrons, while Cosimo I commissioned the Uffizi building as a center of government in the sixteenth century. The family’s story joins finance, politics, and cultural patronage: works created or collected under Medici rule remain central to Florence’s museums.

key_facts.text: The family rose through merchant and banking wealth in fifteenth-century Florence.
Medici patronage supported art and humanist learning.
Family members gained formal ruling titles in the sixteenth century.
Cosimo I commissioned the Uffizi as government offices.
The Uffizi, Pitti Palace, and Boboli Gardens preserve Medici collections and legacy.

overview.text: World War I changed soldiers’ head protection as artillery fragments caused many head injuries. Early-war headwear included the German spiked Pickelhaube, which offered too little protection for trench warfare. France introduced the steel Adrian helmet in 1915, Britain adopted the shallow-brimmed Brodie helmet that September, and Germany introduced its steel Stahlhelm in 1916. Their shapes differed: the Brodie’s broad brim helped shield against falling debris, while the German design covered more of the head and neck. Steel helmets reduced some shrapnel injuries, although the Brodie design left the neck and lower head exposed. The designs became recognizable symbols of the armies that wore them.

key_facts.text: The French Adrian steel helmet was introduced in late 1915.
Britain adopted the Brodie design in September 1915.
The Brodie’s broad brim protected against falling fragments.
The German M16 Stahlhelm entered service in 1916.
The Stahlhelm replaced the spiked leather Pickelhaube.

overview.text: The Darien scheme was a Scottish attempt to establish a trading colony on the Isthmus of Panama in the late 1690s. Backed by the Company of Scotland, its first expedition sailed in 1698 and founded a settlement called New Edinburgh. The colonists hoped the location would open trade between the Atlantic and Pacific worlds, but inadequate supplies, disease, difficult farming, and Spanish opposition undermined the venture. Two expeditions failed, costing many lives and much of the money invested by Scots. The financial disaster became one factor in the negotiations that led to the 1707 union with England; it was not the only cause of that political decision.

key_facts.text: The Company of Scotland organized the colonial venture.
The first expedition sailed from Leith in July 1698.
The settlement was called New Edinburgh.
Spanish forces drove out the second expedition in 1700.
Investor compensation became an issue in union negotiations.

overview.text: Charles X was king of France from 1824 until the July Revolution of 1830 removed him. A younger brother of Louis XVI and Louis XVIII, he returned from exile after the French Revolution and succeeded Louis XVIII. He favored a stronger traditional monarchy and was crowned at Reims in 1825. In July 1830 he issued ordinances restricting press freedom, dissolving the elected chamber, and changing election rules. The measures helped spark three days of revolt in Paris, known as the Three Glorious Days. Charles abdicated and went into exile; Louis-Philippe then became king. His fall showed how sharply the restored monarchy could clash with demands for constitutional limits.

He was crowned at Reims in 1825.
His July 1830 ordinances suspended press freedom.
The ordinances dissolved the Chamber and changed election rules.

overview.text: Byzantine Iconoclasm was a series of disputes over religious images in the Byzantine Empire during the eighth and ninth centuries. Opponents of icons feared that honoring images could become idolatry; defenders distinguished respect shown to an image from worship owed to God. Imperial and church leaders took different sides over time. A council called by Constantine V supported iconoclasm in 754, while the Second Council of Nicaea in 787 approved the veneration of icons. Iconoclast policy returned in the early ninth century before the use of icons was restored in 843. The controversy shaped Byzantine worship and art, although scholars caution that policy and practice varied across the empire.

Constantine V’s Council of Hieria backed iconoclasm in 754.
The Second Council of Nicaea defended icons in 787.
Iconoclast policy revived in 815 and ended in 843.
Scholars caution against treating iconoclasm as uniformly enforced everywhere.
